patterns.title: Functional Separation
patterns.summary: Assign incompatible jobs to different elements, then design the connections they still need.

identity_resolution.decision: New engineering terminal pattern; Function and Architecture is a navigation family, not a parent.
identity_resolution.boundary: Physical function allocation under incompatible operating conditions. Segmentation selects manageable units; process-oriented separation of observation, interpretation, and action concerns reasoning stages, not an engineering element/interface allocation.

use_when: One element must satisfy incompatible environments or working conditions.
Improving one function repeatedly makes another worse.
The conflict path and required surviving interfaces can be identified.
goals: Give each job suitable working conditions
Compare the original conflict with the added interface burden
mechanisms: Allocate jobs to distinct elements or regions
Specify connections for required power, information, force, or material transfer
Control unwanted transfer and verify the operating envelope
not_ideal_when: The functions are compatible and a shared element already meets the duty.
The dominant conflict path remains effectively shared.
The added connection burden defeats the function being protected.
example_user_queries: Our pump needs bearing oil but the process fluid cannot accept it.
Two jobs in the same component keep forcing conflicting design choices.
Should we move the power electronics outside the measurement enclosure?
The reference drifts as the drive cabinet warms up.
We moved the electronics away and the sensor signal became slower.
How do we decide which functions need separate elements?
Can separate functional regions stay in one assembly?
The parts are farther apart but heat still reaches the sensitive structure.
What new problems do we create when we separate the sensor and amplifier?
Should a low-heat sensor front end stay near the measurement point?
How is dividing a machine for service different from separating its jobs?
Which functions must share a connection even after we split them?

related_patterns.title: Segmentation
related_patterns.relationship: Neighbor chooses independently manageable units; physical service boundaries and function allocation can differ. Not a parent.

related_patterns.title: Function Integration
related_patterns.relationship: Combines compatible jobs; can complement separation elsewhere in a system.

related_patterns.title: Disturbance Isolation
related_patterns.relationship: Attenuates unwanted coupling without necessarily reallocating jobs; separation can still require isolation.

related_patterns.title: Isolate Metrology from Working Loads
related_patterns.relationship: Provides an independent structural reference path; moving a heat source does not necessarily provide that path.

worked_examples.name: Pump wet region and lubricated bearing housing
worked_examples.baseline: Chosen bearing lubricant is incompatible with the process-fluid requirement.
worked_examples.intervention: Place lubricated bearings outside the wetted region; retain a continuous shaft through an appropriate casing seal.
worked_examples.evidence: Functional regions and necessary shaft crossing are visible in an original cutaway.
worked_examples.limits: No contamination level, leakage rate, alignment tolerance, seal selection, or pump rating is calculated. Bearing housing seals and intervening space also require design.

worked_examples.name: External power stage for a measuring machine
worked_examples.intervention: Relocate power electronics and cooling outside the reference enclosure.
worked_examples.limits: Uniform temperature and unconstrained expansion. The prescribed temperatures are not predicted outcomes of the relocation. No heat-flow model or material selection.

worked_examples.name: Remote high-impedance sensor
worked_examples.limits: Passive lumped-capacitance model. Settling, not propagation delay. Omits resistance/inductance of cable, input capacitance, leakage, pickup, and active-driver dynamics. No noise or amplifier-stability prediction. A local front end is a design candidate, not a universal repair.

source_notes.basis: Read casing/seal-chamber and power-end descriptions, bearing roles, and oil/grease lubrication arrangements.
source_notes.boundary: Supports component allocation for that model; the original horizontal schematic is not a drawing of this vertical inline product. No manufacturer geometry, operating limit, contamination outcome, or performance figure is reused.

source_notes.basis: Read shaft/casing sealing function, mechanical-seal leakage and heat discussion, and dependence on operating conditions.
source_notes.boundary: Supports an imperfect, condition-dependent boundary. No universal seal selection, operating procedure, or zero-leakage claim.

source_notes.source: Li et al., Machine Tool Thermal Error Measurement and Prediction via Wireless Microscope, 2024
source_notes.basis: Read abstract and introduction identifying structural thermal deformation from internal sources and ambient temperature.
source_notes.boundary: General mechanism only. The cabinet layout and uniform temperature fixtures are hypothetical; no paper measurement, accuracy percentage, or compensation result is transferred.

source_notes.source: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, 1.3 Thermal Expansion
source_notes.basis: Read linear-expansion relation and its use with temperature change.
source_notes.boundary: Coefficient, length, and temperature rises are explicit teaching assumptions; they do not establish a temperature reduction from the cabinet move.

source_notes.source: Analog Devices, Hardware Design Techniques, Section 9, printed pages 86–87 / PDF pages 85–86
source_notes.basis: Read Figures 9.79–9.80 and adjacent discussion of high-impedance remote sensors, cable capacitance, leakage, and nearby preamplification.
source_notes.boundary: Qualitative evidence for interface burden; the numerical passive RC fixture is original and is not a photodiode/transimpedance amplifier model. No source shielding sketch is copied or presented as a universal grounding rule.

source_notes.source: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, 10.5 RC Circuits
source_notes.basis: Read charging relation, exponential limiting behavior, and RC time-constant units.
source_notes.boundary: Simple passive settling only; not a propagation, pickup, transmission-line, or active-driver stability calculation.

research_lead_status.lead: University of Michigan Design Heuristics handout
research_lead_status.status: Not used as evidence; direct PDF fetch returned HTTP 403 during earlier research in this chat. This taxonomy is not represented as its official cards.

research_lead_status.lead: J. E. Gordon, Structures: Or Why Things Don’t Fall Down
research_lead_status.status: Contextual lead only. No specific passage was read for this article, and no claim or illustration is attributed to the book.

graphics.decision: Three static original SVG figures, each with a phone companion; no widget.
graphics.reason: The region allocation, matched thermal layouts, and two explicitly computed settling curves answer fixed questions. An interactive control would add little to these comparisons.
graphics.style: Approved fixed-white editorial engineering drawings; regular Helvetica Neue, fine neutral strokes and restrained green.

figures.learning_question: Which jobs occupy distinct pump regions, and what still connects them?
figures.changed: Bearing lubrication is allocated outside the wetted chamber; a seal manages the shaft penetration.
figures.phone_composition: Same full-width section with larger labels and greater vertical callout spacing.
figures.alt: Pump section shows the wetted impeller chamber on the left, a shaft seal at its right wall, an intervening space, and two bearings in a separate lubricated housing. The continuous shaft crosses these regions.
figures.caption: Original schematic, not to scale. Green arrows show process-fluid flow; the shaft remains a mechanical connection. The shaft seal controls the casing penetration. Separate bearing-housing seals and the intervening space also matter; the drawing does not establish contamination control or seal performance.

figures.learning_question: What changes when the heat-generating power stage leaves the reference enclosure?
figures.changed: The power stage and its cooling path move into an external cabinet; a cable remains.
figures.arrow_meaning: Qualitative heat paths, not computed heat flux
figures.phone_composition: Stacked matched sections retained; greater space between cases and larger labels.
figures.alt: Two stacked machine sections retain the same reference bar and supports. In the first, the power stage shares the measurement enclosure; in the second, it sits in an external cabinet connected by cable, with its cooling path outside.
figures.caption: Matched schematic layouts retain the reference and electrical duty. Arrows indicate qualitative heat paths, not computed heat flux. The separate temperature-sensitivity calculation assumes uniform prescribed temperature rises; relocation alone does not establish a change from 4 K to 1 K.

figures.learning_question: What settling burden can a longer cable impose on a high-impedance sensor?
figures.changed: Cable length changes from 2 m to 20 m.
figures.arrow_meaning: No flow arrows; circuit paths are electrical connections and plot axes show time and received fraction.
figures.phone_composition: Circuit and plot remain stacked, with larger labels and greater circuit-to-plot spacing.
figures.alt: A sensor represented by a voltage source and resistance drives a cable capacitance at the receiver. Computed step-response curves compare the assumed 2 metre and 20 metre cables, marking their different times to reach 90 percent.
figures.caption: Calculated passive RC teaching model: the same 100 kΩ source drives cable capacitance of 100 pF/m. Solid and dashed curves distinguish 2 m and 20 m. This is settling lag, not cable propagation time, a noise prediction, or an amplifier-stability analysis.

graphics.provenance: Original editable schematic geometry and numerically evaluated RC traces. No traced manufacturer/book drawings, borrowed photographs, raster generation, or simulated temperature fields.
